lines.text: Enter Chorus.

lines.speaker: CHORUS
lines.text: Two households, both alike in dignity,

lines.speaker: CHORUS
lines.text: In fair Verona, where we lay our scene,

lines.speaker: CHORUS
lines.text: From ancient grudge break to new mutiny,

lines.speaker: CHORUS
lines.text: Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean.

lines.speaker: CHORUS
lines.text: From forth the fatal loins of these two foes

lines.speaker: CHORUS
lines.text: A pair of star-cross’d lovers take their life;

lines.speaker: CHORUS
lines.text: Whose misadventur’d piteous overthrows

lines.speaker: CHORUS
lines.text: Doth with their death bury their parents’ strife.

lines.speaker: CHORUS
lines.text: The fearful passage of their death-mark’d love,

lines.speaker: CHORUS
lines.text: And the continuance of their parents’ rage,

lines.speaker: CHORUS
lines.text: Which, but their children’s end, nought could remove,

lines.speaker: CHORUS
lines.text: Is now the two hours’ traffic of our stage;

lines.speaker: CHORUS
lines.text: The which, if you with patient ears attend,

lines.speaker: CHORUS
lines.text: What here shall miss, our toil shall strive to mend.
[_Exit._]
Enter Sampson and Gregory armed with swords and bucklers.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: Gregory, on my word, we’ll not carry coals.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: No, for then we should be colliers.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: I mean, if we be in choler, we’ll draw.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: Ay, while you live, draw your neck out o’ the collar.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: I strike quickly, being moved.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: But thou art not quickly moved to strike.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: A dog of the house of Montague moves me.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: To move is to stir; and to be valiant is to stand: therefore, if thou

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: art moved, thou runn’st away.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: A dog of that house shall move me to stand.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: I will take the wall of any man or maid of Montague’s.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: That shows thee a weak slave, for the weakest goes to the wall.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: True, and therefore women, being the weaker vessels, are ever thrust to

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: the wall: therefore I will push Montague’s men from the wall, and

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: thrust his maids to the wall.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: The quarrel is between our masters and us their men.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: ’Tis all one, I will show myself a tyrant: when I have fought with the

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: men I will be civil with the maids, I will cut off their heads.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: The heads of the maids?

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: Ay, the heads of the maids, or their maidenheads; take it in what sense

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: thou wilt.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: They must take it in sense that feel it.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: Me they shall feel while I am able to stand: and ’tis known I am a

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: pretty piece of flesh.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: ’Tis well thou art not fish; if thou hadst, thou hadst been poor John.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: Draw thy tool; here comes of the house of Montagues.
Enter Abram and Balthasar.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: My naked weapon is out: quarrel, I will back thee.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: How? Turn thy back and run?

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: Fear me not.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: No, marry; I fear thee!

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: Let us take the law of our sides; let them begin.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: I will frown as I pass by, and let them take it as they list.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: Nay, as they dare. I will bite my thumb at them, which is disgrace to

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: them if they bear it.

lines.speaker: ABRAM
lines.text: Do you bite your thumb at us, sir?

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: I do bite my thumb, sir.

lines.speaker: ABRAM
lines.text: Do you bite your thumb at us, sir?

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: Is the law of our side if I say ay?

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: No sir, I do not bite my thumb at you, sir; but I bite my thumb, sir.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: Do you quarrel, sir?

lines.speaker: ABRAM
lines.text: Quarrel, sir? No, sir.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: But if you do, sir, I am for you. I serve as good a man as you.

lines.speaker: ABRAM
lines.text: No better.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: Well, sir.
Enter Benvolio.

lines.speaker: GREGORY
lines.text: Say better; here comes one of my master’s kinsmen.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: Yes, better, sir.

lines.speaker: ABRAM
lines.text: You lie.

lines.speaker: SAMPSON
lines.text: Draw, if you be men. Gregory, remember thy washing blow.
[_They fight._]

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Part, fools! put up your swords, you know not what you do.
[_Beats down their swords._]
Enter Tybalt.

lines.speaker: TYBALT
lines.text: What, art thou drawn among these heartless hinds?

lines.speaker: TYBALT
lines.text: Turn thee Benvolio, look upon thy death.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: I do but keep the peace, put up thy sword,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Or manage it to part these men with me.

lines.speaker: TYBALT
lines.text: What, drawn, and talk of peace? I hate the word

lines.speaker: TYBALT
lines.text: As I hate hell, all Montagues, and thee:

lines.speaker: TYBALT
lines.text: Have at thee, coward.
[_They fight._]
Enter three or four Citizens with clubs.

lines.speaker: FIRST CITIZEN
lines.text: Clubs, bills and partisans! Strike! Beat them down!

lines.speaker: FIRST CITIZEN
lines.text: Down with the Capulets! Down with the Montagues!
Enter Capulet in his gown, and Lady Capulet.

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: What noise is this? Give me my long sword, ho!

lines.speaker: LADY CAPULET
lines.text: A crutch, a crutch! Why call you for a sword?

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: My sword, I say! Old Montague is come,

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: And flourishes his blade in spite of me.
Enter Montague and his Lady Montague.

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Thou villain Capulet! Hold me not, let me go.

lines.speaker: LADY MONTAGUE
lines.text: Thou shalt not stir one foot to seek a foe.
Enter Prince Escalus, with Attendants.

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: Rebellious subjects, enemies to peace,

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: Profaners of this neighbour-stained steel,—

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: Will they not hear? What, ho! You men, you beasts,

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: That quench the fire of your pernicious rage

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: With purple fountains issuing from your veins,

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: On pain of torture, from those bloody hands

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: Throw your mistemper’d weapons to the ground

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: And hear the sentence of your moved prince.

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: Three civil brawls, bred of an airy word,

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: By thee, old Capulet, and Montague,

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: Have thrice disturb’d the quiet of our streets,

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: And made Verona’s ancient citizens

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: Cast by their grave beseeming ornaments,

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: To wield old partisans, in hands as old,

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: Canker’d with peace, to part your canker’d hate.

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: If ever you disturb our streets again,

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: Your lives shall pay the forfeit of the peace.

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: For this time all the rest depart away:

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: You, Capulet, shall go along with me,

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: And Montague, come you this afternoon,

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: To know our farther pleasure in this case,

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: To old Free-town, our common judgement-place.

lines.speaker: PRINCE
lines.text: Once more, on pain of death, all men depart.
[_Exeunt Prince and Attendants; Capulet, Lady Capulet, Tybalt, Citizens and Servants._]

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Who set this ancient quarrel new abroach?

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Speak, nephew, were you by when it began?

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Here were the servants of your adversary

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: And yours, close fighting ere I did approach.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: I drew to part them, in the instant came

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: The fiery Tybalt, with his sword prepar’d,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Which, as he breath’d defiance to my ears,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: He swung about his head, and cut the winds,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Who nothing hurt withal, hiss’d him in scorn.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: While we were interchanging thrusts and blows

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Came more and more, and fought on part and part,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Till the Prince came, who parted either part.

lines.speaker: LADY MONTAGUE
lines.text: O where is Romeo, saw you him today?

lines.speaker: LADY MONTAGUE
lines.text: Right glad I am he was not at this fray.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Madam, an hour before the worshipp’d sun

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Peer’d forth the golden window of the east,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: A troubled mind drave me to walk abroad,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Where underneath the grove of sycamore

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: That westward rooteth from this city side,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: So early walking did I see your son.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Towards him I made, but he was ware of me,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: And stole into the covert of the wood.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: I, measuring his affections by my own,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Which then most sought where most might not be found,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Being one too many by my weary self,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Pursu’d my humour, not pursuing his,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: And gladly shunn’d who gladly fled from me.

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Many a morning hath he there been seen,

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: With tears augmenting the fresh morning’s dew,

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Adding to clouds more clouds with his deep sighs;

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: But all so soon as the all-cheering sun

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Should in the farthest east begin to draw

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: The shady curtains from Aurora’s bed,

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Away from light steals home my heavy son,

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: And private in his chamber pens himself,

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Shuts up his windows, locks fair daylight out

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: And makes himself an artificial night.

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Black and portentous must this humour prove,

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Unless good counsel may the cause remove.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: My noble uncle, do you know the cause?

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: I neither know it nor can learn of him.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Have you importun’d him by any means?

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Both by myself and many other friends;

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: But he, his own affections’ counsellor,

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Is to himself—I will not say how true—

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: But to himself so secret and so close,

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: So far from sounding and discovery,

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: As is the bud bit with an envious worm

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Ere he can spread his sweet leaves to the air,

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Or dedicate his beauty to the sun.

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: Could we but learn from whence his sorrows grow,

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: We would as willingly give cure as know.
Enter Romeo.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: See, where he comes. So please you step aside;

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: I’ll know his grievance or be much denied.

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: I would thou wert so happy by thy stay

lines.speaker: MONTAGUE
lines.text: To hear true shrift. Come, madam, let’s away,
[_Exeunt Montague and Lady Montague._]

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Good morrow, cousin.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Is the day so young?

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: But new struck nine.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Ay me, sad hours seem long.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Was that my father that went hence so fast?

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: It was. What sadness lengthens Romeo’s hours?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Not having that which, having, makes them short.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: In love?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Out.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Of love?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Out of her favour where I am in love.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Alas that love so gentle in his view,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Should be so tyrannous and rough in proof.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Alas that love, whose view is muffled still,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Should, without eyes, see pathways to his will!

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Where shall we dine? O me! What fray was here?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Yet tell me not, for I have heard it all.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Here’s much to do with hate, but more with love:

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Why, then, O brawling love! O loving hate!

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: O anything, of nothing first create!

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: O heavy lightness! serious vanity!

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Misshapen chaos of well-seeming forms!

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Feather of lead, bright smoke, cold fire, sick health!

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Still-waking sleep, that is not what it is!

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: This love feel I, that feel no love in this.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Dost thou not laugh?

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: No coz, I rather weep.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Good heart, at what?

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: At thy good heart’s oppression.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Why such is love’s transgression.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Griefs of mine own lie heavy in my breast,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Which thou wilt propagate to have it prest

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: With more of thine. This love that thou hast shown

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Doth add more grief to too much of mine own.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Love is a smoke made with the fume of sighs;

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Being purg’d, a fire sparkling in lovers’ eyes;

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Being vex’d, a sea nourish’d with lovers’ tears:

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: What is it else? A madness most discreet,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: A choking gall, and a preserving sweet.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Farewell, my coz.
[_Going._]

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Soft! I will go along:

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: And if you leave me so, you do me wrong.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Tut! I have lost myself; I am not here.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: This is not Romeo, he’s some other where.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Tell me in sadness who is that you love?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: What, shall I groan and tell thee?

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Groan! Why, no; but sadly tell me who.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Bid a sick man in sadness make his will,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: A word ill urg’d to one that is so ill.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: In sadness, cousin, I do love a woman.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: I aim’d so near when I suppos’d you lov’d.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: A right good markman, and she’s fair I love.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: A right fair mark, fair coz, is soonest hit.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Well, in that hit you miss: she’ll not be hit

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: With Cupid’s arrow, she hath Dian’s wit;

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: And in strong proof of chastity well arm’d,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: From love’s weak childish bow she lives uncharm’d.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: She will not stay the siege of loving terms

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Nor bide th’encounter of assailing eyes,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Nor ope her lap to saint-seducing gold:

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: O she’s rich in beauty, only poor

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: That when she dies, with beauty dies her store.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Then she hath sworn that she will still live chaste?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: She hath, and in that sparing makes huge waste;

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: For beauty starv’d with her severity,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Cuts beauty off from all posterity.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: She is too fair, too wise; wisely too fair,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: To merit bliss by making me despair.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: She hath forsworn to love, and in that vow

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Do I live dead, that live to tell it now.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Be rul’d by me, forget to think of her.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: O teach me how I should forget to think.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: By giving liberty unto thine eyes;

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Examine other beauties.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: ’Tis the way

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: To call hers, exquisite, in question more.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: These happy masks that kiss fair ladies’ brows,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Being black, puts us in mind they hide the fair;

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: He that is strucken blind cannot forget

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: The precious treasure of his eyesight lost.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Show me a mistress that is passing fair,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: What doth her beauty serve but as a note

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Where I may read who pass’d that passing fair?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Farewell, thou canst not teach me to forget.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: I’ll pay that doctrine, or else die in debt.
[_Exeunt._]
Enter Capulet, Paris and Servant.

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: But Montague is bound as well as I,

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: In penalty alike; and ’tis not hard, I think,

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: For men so old as we to keep the peace.

lines.speaker: PARIS
lines.text: Of honourable reckoning are you both,

lines.speaker: PARIS
lines.text: And pity ’tis you liv’d at odds so long.

lines.speaker: PARIS
lines.text: But now my lord, what say you to my suit?

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: But saying o’er what I have said before.

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: My child is yet a stranger in the world,

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: She hath not seen the change of fourteen years;

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: Let two more summers wither in their pride

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: Ere we may think her ripe to be a bride.

lines.speaker: PARIS
lines.text: Younger than she are happy mothers made.

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: And too soon marr’d are those so early made.

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: The earth hath swallowed all my hopes but she,

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: She is the hopeful lady of my earth:

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: But woo her, gentle Paris, get her heart,

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: My will to her consent is but a part;

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: And she agree, within her scope of choice

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: Lies my consent and fair according voice.

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: This night I hold an old accustom’d feast,

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: Whereto I have invited many a guest,

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: Such as I love, and you among the store,

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: One more, most welcome, makes my number more.

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: At my poor house look to behold this night

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: Earth-treading stars that make dark heaven light:

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: Such comfort as do lusty young men feel

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: When well apparell’d April on the heel

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: Of limping winter treads, even such delight

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: Among fresh female buds shall you this night

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: Inherit at my house. Hear all, all see,

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: And like her most whose merit most shall be:

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: Which, on more view of many, mine, being one,

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: May stand in number, though in reckoning none.

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: Come, go with me. Go, sirrah, trudge about

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: Through fair Verona; find those persons out

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: Whose names are written there, [_gives a paper_] and to them say,

lines.speaker: CAPULET
lines.text: My house and welcome on their pleasure stay.
[_Exeunt Capulet and Paris._]

lines.speaker: SERVANT
lines.text: Find them out whose names are written here! It is written that the

lines.speaker: SERVANT
lines.text: shoemaker should meddle with his yard and the tailor with his last, the

lines.speaker: SERVANT

lines.text: And but thou love me, let them find me here.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: My life were better ended by their hate

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Than death prorogued, wanting of thy love.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: By whose direction found’st thou out this place?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: By love, that first did prompt me to enquire;

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: He lent me counsel, and I lent him eyes.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: I am no pilot; yet wert thou as far

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: As that vast shore wash’d with the farthest sea,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: I should adventure for such merchandise.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Thou knowest the mask of night is on my face,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Else would a maiden blush bepaint my cheek

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: For that which thou hast heard me speak tonight.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Fain would I dwell on form, fain, fain deny

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: What I have spoke; but farewell compliment.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Dost thou love me? I know thou wilt say Ay,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: And I will take thy word. Yet, if thou swear’st,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Thou mayst prove false. At lovers’ perjuries,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: They say Jove laughs. O gentle Romeo,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: If thou dost love, pronounce it faithfully.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Or if thou thinkest I am too quickly won,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: I’ll frown and be perverse, and say thee nay,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: So thou wilt woo. But else, not for the world.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: In truth, fair Montague, I am too fond;

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: And therefore thou mayst think my ’haviour light:

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: But trust me, gentleman, I’ll prove more true

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Than those that have more cunning to be strange.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: I should have been more strange, I must confess,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: But that thou overheard’st, ere I was ’ware,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: My true-love passion; therefore pardon me,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: And not impute this yielding to light love,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Which the dark night hath so discovered.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Lady, by yonder blessed moon I vow,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: That tips with silver all these fruit-tree tops,—

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: O swear not by the moon, th’inconstant moon,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: That monthly changes in her circled orb,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Lest that thy love prove likewise variable.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: What shall I swear by?

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Do not swear at all.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Or if thou wilt, swear by thy gracious self,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Which is the god of my idolatry,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: And I’ll believe thee.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: If my heart’s dear love,—

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Well, do not swear. Although I joy in thee,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: I have no joy of this contract tonight;

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: It is too rash, too unadvis’d, too sudden,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Too like the lightning, which doth cease to be

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Ere one can say “It lightens.” Sweet, good night.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: This bud of love, by summer’s ripening breath,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: May prove a beauteous flower when next we meet.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Good night, good night. As sweet repose and rest

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Come to thy heart as that within my breast.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: O wilt thou leave me so unsatisfied?

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: What satisfaction canst thou have tonight?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Th’exchange of thy love’s faithful vow for mine.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: I gave thee mine before thou didst request it;

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: And yet I would it were to give again.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Would’st thou withdraw it? For what purpose, love?

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: But to be frank and give it thee again.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: And yet I wish but for the thing I have;

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: My bounty is as boundless as the sea,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: My love as deep; the more I give to thee,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: The more I have, for both are infinite.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: I hear some noise within. Dear love, adieu.
[_Nurse calls within._]

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Anon, good Nurse!—Sweet Montague be true.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Stay but a little, I will come again.
[_Exit._]

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: O blessed, blessed night. I am afeard,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Being in night, all this is but a dream,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Too flattering sweet to be substantial.
Enter Juliet above.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Three words, dear Romeo, and good night indeed.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: If that thy bent of love be honourable,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Thy purpose marriage, send me word tomorrow,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: By one that I’ll procure to come to thee,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Where and what time thou wilt perform the rite,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: And all my fortunes at thy foot I’ll lay

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: And follow thee my lord throughout the world.
[_Within._]

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Madam.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: I come, anon.— But if thou meanest not well,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: I do beseech thee,—
[_Within._]

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Madam.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: By and by I come—

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: To cease thy strife and leave me to my grief.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Tomorrow will I send.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: So thrive my soul,—

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: A thousand times good night.
[_Exit._]

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: A thousand times the worse, to want thy light.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Love goes toward love as schoolboys from their books,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: But love from love, towards school with heavy looks.
[_Retiring slowly._]
Re-enter Juliet, above.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Hist! Romeo, hist! O for a falconer’s voice

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: To lure this tassel-gentle back again.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Bondage is hoarse and may not speak aloud,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Else would I tear the cave where Echo lies,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: And make her airy tongue more hoarse than mine

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: With repetition of my Romeo’s name.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: It is my soul that calls upon my name.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: How silver-sweet sound lovers’ tongues by night,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Like softest music to attending ears.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Romeo.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: My dear?

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: What o’clock tomorrow

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Shall I send to thee?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: By the hour of nine.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: I will not fail. ’Tis twenty years till then.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: I have forgot why I did call thee back.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Let me stand here till thou remember it.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: I shall forget, to have thee still stand there,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Remembering how I love thy company.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: And I’ll still stay, to have thee still forget,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Forgetting any other home but this.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: ’Tis almost morning; I would have thee gone,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: And yet no farther than a wanton’s bird,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: That lets it hop a little from her hand,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Like a poor prisoner in his twisted gyves,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: And with a silk thread plucks it back again,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: So loving-jealous of his liberty.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: I would I were thy bird.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Sweet, so would I:

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Yet I should kill thee with much cherishing.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Good night, good night. Parting is such sweet sorrow

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: That I shall say good night till it be morrow.
[_Exit._]

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Sleep dwell upon thine eyes, peace in thy breast.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Would I were sleep and peace, so sweet to rest.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Hence will I to my ghostly Sire’s cell,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: His help to crave and my dear hap to tell.
[_Exit._]
Enter Friar Lawrence with a basket.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: The grey-ey’d morn smiles on the frowning night,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Chequering the eastern clouds with streaks of light;

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: And fleckled darkness like a drunkard reels

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: From forth day’s pathway, made by Titan’s fiery wheels

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Now, ere the sun advance his burning eye,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: The day to cheer, and night’s dank dew to dry,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: I must upfill this osier cage of ours

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: With baleful weeds and precious-juiced flowers.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: The earth that’s nature’s mother, is her tomb;

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: What is her burying grave, that is her womb:

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: And from her womb children of divers kind

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: We sucking on her natural bosom find.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Many for many virtues excellent,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: None but for some, and yet all different.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: O, mickle is the powerful grace that lies

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: In plants, herbs, stones, and their true qualities.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: For naught so vile that on the earth doth live

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: But to the earth some special good doth give;

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Nor aught so good but, strain’d from that fair use,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Revolts from true birth, stumbling on abuse.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Virtue itself turns vice being misapplied,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: And vice sometime’s by action dignified.
Enter Romeo.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Within the infant rind of this weak flower

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Poison hath residence, and medicine power:

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: For this, being smelt, with that part cheers each part;

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Being tasted, slays all senses with the heart.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Two such opposed kings encamp them still

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: In man as well as herbs,—grace and rude will;

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: And where the worser is predominant,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Full soon the canker death eats up that plant.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Good morrow, father.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Benedicite!

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: What early tongue so sweet saluteth me?

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Young son, it argues a distemper’d head

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: So soon to bid good morrow to thy bed.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Care keeps his watch in every old man’s eye,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: And where care lodges sleep will never lie;

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: But where unbruised youth with unstuff’d brain

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Doth couch his limbs, there golden sleep doth reign.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Therefore thy earliness doth me assure

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Thou art uprous’d with some distemperature;

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Or if not so, then here I hit it right,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Our Romeo hath not been in bed tonight.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: That last is true; the sweeter rest was mine.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: God pardon sin. Wast thou with Rosaline?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: With Rosaline, my ghostly father? No.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: I have forgot that name, and that name’s woe.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: That’s my good son. But where hast thou been then?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: I’ll tell thee ere thou ask it me again.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: I have been feasting with mine enemy,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Where on a sudden one hath wounded me

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: That’s by me wounded. Both our remedies

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Within thy help and holy physic lies.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: I bear no hatred, blessed man; for lo,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: My intercession likewise steads my foe.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Be plain, good son, and homely in thy drift;

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Riddling confession finds but riddling shrift.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Then plainly know my heart’s dear love is set

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: On the fair daughter of rich Capulet.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: As mine on hers, so hers is set on mine;

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: And all combin’d, save what thou must combine

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: By holy marriage. When, and where, and how

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: We met, we woo’d, and made exchange of vow,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: I’ll tell thee as we pass; but this I pray,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: That thou consent to marry us today.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Holy Saint Francis! What a change is here!

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Is Rosaline, that thou didst love so dear,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: So soon forsaken? Young men’s love then lies

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Not truly in their hearts, but in their eyes.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Jesu Maria, what a deal of brine

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Hath wash’d thy sallow cheeks for Rosaline!

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: How much salt water thrown away in waste,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: To season love, that of it doth not taste.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: The sun not yet thy sighs from heaven clears,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Thy old groans yet ring in mine ancient ears.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Lo here upon thy cheek the stain doth sit

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Of an old tear that is not wash’d off yet.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: If ere thou wast thyself, and these woes thine,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Thou and these woes were all for Rosaline,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: And art thou chang’d? Pronounce this sentence then,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Women may fall, when there’s no strength in men.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Thou chidd’st me oft for loving Rosaline.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: For doting, not for loving, pupil mine.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: And bad’st me bury love.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Not in a grave

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: To lay one in, another out to have.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: I pray thee chide me not, her I love now

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Doth grace for grace and love for love allow.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: The other did not so.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: O, she knew well

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Thy love did read by rote, that could not spell.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: But come young waverer, come go with me,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: In one respect I’ll thy assistant be;

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: For this alliance may so happy prove,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: To turn your households’ rancour to pure love.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: O let us hence; I stand on sudden haste.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast.
[_Exeunt._]
Enter Benvolio and Mercutio.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Where the devil should this Romeo be? Came he not home tonight?

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Not to his father’s; I spoke with his man.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Why, that same pale hard-hearted wench, that Rosaline, torments him so

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: that he will sure run mad.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Tybalt, the kinsman to old Capulet, hath sent a letter to his father’s

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: house.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: A challenge, on my life.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Romeo will answer it.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Any man that can write may answer a letter.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Nay, he will answer the letter’s master, how he dares, being dared.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Alas poor Romeo, he is already dead, stabbed with a white wench’s black

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: eye; run through the ear with a love song, the very pin of his heart

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: cleft with the blind bow-boy’s butt-shaft. And is he a man to encounter

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Tybalt?

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Why, what is Tybalt?

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: More than Prince of cats. O, he’s the courageous captain of

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: compliments. He fights as you sing prick-song, keeps time, distance,

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: and proportion. He rests his minim rest, one, two, and the third in

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: your bosom: the very butcher of a silk button, a duellist, a duellist;

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: a gentleman of the very first house, of the first and second cause. Ah,

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: the immortal passado, the punto reverso, the hay.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: The what?

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: The pox of such antic lisping, affecting phantasies; these new tuners

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: of accent. By Jesu, a very good blade, a very tall man, a very good

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: whore. Why, is not this a lamentable thing, grandsire, that we should

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: be thus afflicted with these strange flies, these fashion-mongers,

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: these pardon-me’s, who stand so much on the new form that they cannot

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: sit at ease on the old bench? O their bones, their bones!
Enter Romeo.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Here comes Romeo, here comes Romeo!

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Without his roe, like a dried herring. O flesh, flesh, how art thou

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: fishified! Now is he for the numbers that Petrarch flowed in. Laura, to

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: his lady, was but a kitchen wench,—marry, she had a better love to

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: berhyme her: Dido a dowdy; Cleopatra a gypsy; Helen and Hero hildings

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: and harlots; Thisbe a grey eye or so, but not to the purpose. Signior

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Romeo, bonjour! There’s a French salutation to your French slop. You

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: gave us the counterfeit fairly last night.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Good morrow to you both. What counterfeit did I give you?

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: The slip sir, the slip; can you not conceive?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Pardon, good Mercutio, my business was great, and in such a case as

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: mine a man may strain courtesy.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: That’s as much as to say, such a case as yours constrains a man to bow

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: in the hams.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Meaning, to curtsy.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Thou hast most kindly hit it.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: A most courteous exposition.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Nay, I am the very pink of courtesy.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Pink for flower.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Right.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Why, then is my pump well flowered.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Sure wit, follow me this jest now, till thou hast worn out thy pump,

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: that when the single sole of it is worn, the jest may remain after the

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: wearing, solely singular.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: O single-soled jest, solely singular for the singleness!

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Come between us, good Benvolio; my wits faint.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Swits and spurs, swits and spurs; or I’ll cry a match.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Nay, if thy wits run the wild-goose chase, I am done. For thou hast

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: more of the wild-goose in one of thy wits, than I am sure, I have in my

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: whole five. Was I with you there for the goose?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Thou wast never with me for anything, when thou wast not there for the

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: goose.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: I will bite thee by the ear for that jest.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Nay, good goose, bite not.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Thy wit is a very bitter sweeting, it is a most sharp sauce.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: And is it not then well served in to a sweet goose?

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: O here’s a wit of cheveril, that stretches from an inch narrow to an

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: ell broad.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: I stretch it out for that word broad, which added to the goose, proves

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: thee far and wide a broad goose.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Why, is not this better now than groaning for love? Now art thou

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: sociable, now art thou Romeo; now art thou what thou art, by art as

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: well as by nature. For this drivelling love is like a great natural,

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: that runs lolling up and down to hide his bauble in a hole.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Stop there, stop there.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Thou desirest me to stop in my tale against the hair.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Thou wouldst else have made thy tale large.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: O, thou art deceived; I would have made it short, for I was come to the

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: whole depth of my tale, and meant indeed to occupy the argument no

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: longer.
Enter Nurse and Peter.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Here’s goodly gear!

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: A sail, a sail!

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Two, two; a shirt and a smock.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Peter!

lines.speaker: PETER
lines.text: Anon.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: My fan, Peter.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Good Peter, to hide her face; for her fan’s the fairer face.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: God ye good morrow, gentlemen.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: God ye good-den, fair gentlewoman.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Is it good-den?

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: ’Tis no less, I tell ye; for the bawdy hand of the dial is now upon the

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: prick of noon.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Out upon you! What a man are you?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: One, gentlewoman, that God hath made for himself to mar.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: By my troth, it is well said; for himself to mar, quoth a? Gentlemen,

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: can any of you tell me where I may find the young Romeo?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: I can tell you: but young Romeo will be older when you have found him

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: than he was when you sought him. I am the youngest of that name, for

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: fault of a worse.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: You say well.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Yea, is the worst well? Very well took, i’faith; wisely, wisely.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: If you be he, sir, I desire some confidence with you.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: She will endite him to some supper.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: A bawd, a bawd, a bawd! So ho!

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: What hast thou found?

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: No hare, sir; unless a hare, sir, in a lenten pie, that is something

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: stale and hoar ere it be spent.
[_Sings._]

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: An old hare hoar,

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: And an old hare hoar,

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Is very good meat in Lent;

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: But a hare that is hoar

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Is too much for a score

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: When it hoars ere it be spent.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Romeo, will you come to your father’s? We’ll to dinner thither.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: I will follow you.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Farewell, ancient lady; farewell, lady, lady, lady.
[_Exeunt Mercutio and Benvolio._]

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: I pray you, sir, what saucy merchant was this that was so full of his

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: ropery?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: A gentleman, Nurse, that loves to hear himself talk, and will speak

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: more in a minute than he will stand to in a month.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: And a speak anything against me, I’ll take him down, and a were lustier

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: than he is, and twenty such Jacks. And if I cannot, I’ll find those

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: that shall. Scurvy knave! I am none of his flirt-gills; I am none of

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: his skains-mates.—And thou must stand by too and suffer every knave to

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: use me at his pleasure!

lines.speaker: PETER
lines.text: I saw no man use you at his pleasure; if I had, my weapon should

lines.speaker: PETER
lines.text: quickly have been out. I warrant you, I dare draw as soon as another

lines.speaker: PETER
lines.text: man, if I see occasion in a good quarrel, and the law on my side.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Now, afore God, I am so vexed that every part about me quivers. Scurvy

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: knave. Pray you, sir, a word: and as I told you, my young lady bid me

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: enquire you out; what she bade me say, I will keep to myself. But first

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: let me tell ye, if ye should lead her in a fool’s paradise, as they

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: say, it were a very gross kind of behaviour, as they say; for the

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: gentlewoman is young. And therefore, if you should deal double with

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: her, truly it were an ill thing to be offered to any gentlewoman, and

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: very weak dealing.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Nurse, commend me to thy lady and mistress. I protest unto

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: thee,—

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Good heart, and i’faith I will tell her as much. Lord, Lord, she will

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: be a joyful woman.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: What wilt thou tell her, Nurse? Thou dost not mark me.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: I will tell her, sir, that you do protest, which, as I take it, is a

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: gentlemanlike offer.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Bid her devise

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Some means to come to shrift this afternoon,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: And there she shall at Friar Lawrence’ cell

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Be shriv’d and married. Here is for thy pains.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: No truly, sir; not a penny.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Go to; I say you shall.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: This afternoon, sir? Well, she shall be there.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: And stay, good Nurse, behind the abbey wall.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Within this hour my man shall be with thee,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: And bring thee cords made like a tackled stair,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Which to the high topgallant of my joy

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Must be my convoy in the secret night.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Farewell, be trusty, and I’ll quit thy pains;

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Farewell; commend me to thy mistress.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Now God in heaven bless thee. Hark you, sir.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: What say’st thou, my dear Nurse?

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Is your man secret? Did you ne’er hear say,

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Two may keep counsel, putting one away?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: I warrant thee my man’s as true as steel.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Well, sir, my mistress is the sweetest lady. Lord, Lord! When ’twas a

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: little prating thing,—O, there is a nobleman in town, one Paris, that

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: would fain lay knife aboard; but she, good soul, had as lief see a

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: toad, a very toad, as see him. I anger her sometimes, and tell her that

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Paris is the properer man, but I’ll warrant you, when I say so, she

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: looks as pale as any clout in the versal world. Doth not rosemary and

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Romeo begin both with a letter?

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Ay, Nurse; what of that? Both with an R.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Ah, mocker! That’s the dog’s name. R is for the—no, I know it begins

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: with some other letter, and she hath the prettiest sententious of it,

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: of you and rosemary, that it would do you good to hear it.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Commend me to thy lady.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Ay, a thousand times. Peter!
[_Exit Romeo._]

lines.speaker: PETER
lines.text: Anon.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Before and apace.
[_Exeunt._]
Enter Juliet.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: The clock struck nine when I did send the Nurse,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: In half an hour she promised to return.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Perchance she cannot meet him. That’s not so.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: O, she is lame. Love’s heralds should be thoughts,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Which ten times faster glides than the sun’s beams,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Driving back shadows over lowering hills:

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Therefore do nimble-pinion’d doves draw love,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: And therefore hath the wind-swift Cupid wings.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Now is the sun upon the highmost hill

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Of this day’s journey, and from nine till twelve

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Is three long hours, yet she is not come.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Had she affections and warm youthful blood,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: She’d be as swift in motion as a ball;

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: My words would bandy her to my sweet love,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: And his to me.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: But old folks, many feign as they were dead;

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Unwieldy, slow, heavy and pale as lead.
Enter Nurse and Peter.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: O God, she comes. O honey Nurse, what news?

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Hast thou met with him? Send thy man away.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Peter, stay at the gate.
[_Exit Peter._]

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Now, good sweet Nurse,—O Lord, why look’st thou sad?

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Though news be sad, yet tell them merrily;

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: If good, thou sham’st the music of sweet news

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: By playing it to me with so sour a face.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: I am aweary, give me leave awhile;

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Fie, how my bones ache! What a jaunt have I had!

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: I would thou hadst my bones, and I thy news:

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Nay come, I pray thee speak; good, good Nurse, speak.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Jesu, what haste? Can you not stay a while? Do you not see that I am

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: out of breath?

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: How art thou out of breath, when thou hast breath

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: To say to me that thou art out of breath?

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: The excuse that thou dost make in this delay

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Is longer than the tale thou dost excuse.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Is thy news good or bad? Answer to that;

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Say either, and I’ll stay the circumstance.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Let me be satisfied, is’t good or bad?

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Well, you have made a simple choice; you know not how to choose a man.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Romeo? No, not he. Though his face be better than any man’s, yet his

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: leg excels all men’s, and for a hand and a foot, and a body, though

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: they be not to be talked on, yet they are past compare. He is not the

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: flower of courtesy, but I’ll warrant him as gentle as a lamb. Go thy

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: ways, wench, serve God. What, have you dined at home?

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: No, no. But all this did I know before.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: What says he of our marriage? What of that?

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Lord, how my head aches! What a head have I!

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: It beats as it would fall in twenty pieces.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: My back o’ t’other side,—O my back, my back!

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Beshrew your heart for sending me about

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: To catch my death with jauncing up and down.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: I’faith, I am sorry that thou art not well.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Sweet, sweet, sweet Nurse, tell me, what says my love?

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Your love says like an honest gentleman,

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: And a courteous, and a kind, and a handsome,

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: And I warrant a virtuous,—Where is your mother?

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Where is my mother? Why, she is within.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Where should she be? How oddly thou repliest.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: ‘Your love says, like an honest gentleman,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: ‘Where is your mother?’

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: O God’s lady dear,

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Are you so hot? Marry, come up, I trow.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Is this the poultice for my aching bones?

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Henceforward do your messages yourself.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Here’s such a coil. Come, what says Romeo?

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Have you got leave to go to shrift today?

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: I have.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Then hie you hence to Friar Lawrence’ cell;

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: There stays a husband to make you a wife.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Now comes the wanton blood up in your cheeks,

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: They’ll be in scarlet straight at any news.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Hie you to church. I must another way,

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: To fetch a ladder by the which your love

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Must climb a bird’s nest soon when it is dark.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: I am the drudge, and toil in your delight;

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: But you shall bear the burden soon at night.

lines.speaker: NURSE
lines.text: Go. I’ll to dinner; hie you to the cell.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Hie to high fortune! Honest Nurse, farewell.
[_Exeunt._]
Enter Friar Lawrence and Romeo.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: So smile the heavens upon this holy act

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: That after-hours with sorrow chide us not.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Amen, amen, but come what sorrow can,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: It cannot countervail the exchange of joy

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: That one short minute gives me in her sight.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Do thou but close our hands with holy words,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Then love-devouring death do what he dare,

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: It is enough I may but call her mine.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: These violent delights have violent ends,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: And in their triumph die; like fire and powder,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Which as they kiss consume. The sweetest honey

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Is loathsome in his own deliciousness,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: And in the taste confounds the appetite.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Therefore love moderately: long love doth so;

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Too swift arrives as tardy as too slow.
Enter Juliet.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Here comes the lady. O, so light a foot

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Will ne’er wear out the everlasting flint.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: A lover may bestride the gossamers

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: That idles in the wanton summer air

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: And yet not fall; so light is vanity.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Good even to my ghostly confessor.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Romeo shall thank thee, daughter, for us both.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: As much to him, else is his thanks too much.

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Ah, Juliet, if the measure of thy joy

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Be heap’d like mine, and that thy skill be more

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: To blazon it, then sweeten with thy breath

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: This neighbour air, and let rich music’s tongue

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Unfold the imagin’d happiness that both

lines.speaker: ROMEO
lines.text: Receive in either by this dear encounter.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Conceit more rich in matter than in words,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: Brags of his substance, not of ornament.

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: They are but beggars that can count their worth;

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: But my true love is grown to such excess,

lines.speaker: JULIET
lines.text: I cannot sum up sum of half my wealth.

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Come, come with me, and we will make short work,

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: For, by your leaves, you shall not stay alone

lines.speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
lines.text: Till holy church incorporate two in one.
[_Exeunt._]
Enter Mercutio, Benvolio, Page and Servants.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: I pray thee, good Mercutio, let’s retire:

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: The day is hot, the Capulets abroad,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: And if we meet, we shall not scape a brawl,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: For now these hot days, is the mad blood stirring.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Thou art like one of these fellows that, when he enters the confines of

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: a tavern, claps me his sword upon the table, and says ‘God send me no

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: need of thee!’ and by the operation of the second cup draws him on the

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: drawer, when indeed there is no need.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Am I like such a fellow?

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Come, come, thou art as hot a Jack in thy mood as any in Italy; and as

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: soon moved to be moody, and as soon moody to be moved.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: And what to?

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Nay, an there were two such, we should have none shortly, for one would

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: kill the other. Thou? Why, thou wilt quarrel with a man that hath a

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: hair more or a hair less in his beard than thou hast. Thou wilt quarrel

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: with a man for cracking nuts, having no other reason but because thou

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: hast hazel eyes. What eye but such an eye would spy out such a quarrel?

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Thy head is as full of quarrels as an egg is full of meat, and yet thy

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: head hath been beaten as addle as an egg for quarrelling. Thou hast

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: quarrelled with a man for coughing in the street, because he hath

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: wakened thy dog that hath lain asleep in the sun. Didst thou not fall

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: out with a tailor for wearing his new doublet before Easter? with

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: another for tying his new shoes with an old riband? And yet thou wilt

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: tutor me from quarrelling!

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: And I were so apt to quarrel as thou art, any man should buy the fee

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: simple of my life for an hour and a quarter.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: The fee simple! O simple!
Enter Tybalt and others.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: By my head, here comes the Capulets.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: By my heel, I care not.

lines.speaker: TYBALT
lines.text: Follow me close, for I will speak to them.

lines.speaker: TYBALT
lines.text: Gentlemen, good-den: a word with one of you.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: And but one word with one of us? Couple it with something; make it a

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: word and a blow.

lines.speaker: TYBALT
lines.text: You shall find me apt enough to that, sir, and you will give me

lines.speaker: TYBALT
lines.text: occasion.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Could you not take some occasion without giving?

lines.speaker: TYBALT
lines.text: Mercutio, thou consortest with Romeo.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Consort? What, dost thou make us minstrels? And thou make minstrels of

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: us, look to hear nothing but discords. Here’s my fiddlestick, here’s

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: that shall make you dance. Zounds, consort!

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: We talk here in the public haunt of men.

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Either withdraw unto some private place,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: And reason coldly of your grievances,

lines.speaker: BENVOLIO
lines.text: Or else depart; here all eyes gaze on us.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Men’s eyes were made to look, and let them gaze.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: I will not budge for no man’s pleasure, I.
Enter Romeo.

lines.speaker: TYBALT
lines.text: Well, peace be with you, sir, here comes my man.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: But I’ll be hanged, sir, if he wear your livery.

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
lines.text: Marry, go before to field, he’ll be your follower;

lines.speaker: MERCUTIO
